source: Kolodner & Barsalou (c.1982) Psychological issues raised by an AI model of reconstructive memory
finding: Kolodner herself lists the E-MOP design as untested against human data. CYRUS organises episodes under generic norms and indexes each episode by how it differs from the norms. A new E-MOP forms when two episodes get the same index.
numbers: No effect sizes. Many open empirical questions are listed (content dependence of elaboration, whether events are the basic unit, whether generic and episodic memory are separate).
limits: Authors say the model was incomplete and was filled in on the basis of intuition. Psychological validity was a plan, not a result.
agent_relevance: The founding design was never tested against people. Use it as a design pattern, not as evidence that it works.

source: Kolodner & Barsalou (c.1982) Psychological issues raised by an AI model of reconstructive memory
finding: Generalisation from only two episodes can be wrong. The design lets later episodes refine norms, or demote norms back to indices.
numbers: Rule: norms = similarities of the first two episodes, later episodes revise. No error rates given.
limits: Early generalisation from two cases is a known risk; the paper offers repair, not a measured error rate.
agent_relevance: Keep generalised lessons marked provisional until several cases back them, and let new cases demote them (fits G3).

source: Kolodner & Barsalou (c.1982) Psychological issues raised by an AI model of reconstructive memory
finding: Retrieval in CYRUS only follows an index if the cue specifies it. When the cue is too thin, the system infers plausible features (for example, a meeting with Begin was probably in Jerusalem). This inference can cause false starts and confusions.
numbers: Three recovery strategies: trigger a schema, infer missing index features, use related events.
limits: The inference step is the same mechanism that causes human-like confusions. It is both the aid and the error source.
agent_relevance: Query expansion for memory search needs a check: inferred cue features are guesses, not facts.

source: Dehn (c.1981) Memory in story invention (AUTHOR program)
finding: Reminding is claimed to arise as a side effect of reconstructive memory: a memory is stored where its expectations were violated, so later inputs sharing that structure recall it. Claimed as useful but not reliably so.
numbers: No experiments. The text says one can never rely on getting a useful reminding.
limits: Pure theory paper. The claim that reminding is very common is an assertion.
agent_relevance: Cross-case reminders are a bonus, not a mechanism to depend on. Schedule explicit retrieval at known impasses.

source: Kolodner (1983) Maintaining organization in a dynamic long-term memory, Cognitive Science 7(4)
finding: Abstract: a knowledge-based method to reorganise memory when unexpected items arrive, with directed generalisation and generalisation refinement. CYRUS is a fact-retrieval system built on it. Retrieval failures arise when memory structure changes over time.
numbers: No numbers in abstract. Full text not opened (HTTP 403).
limits: Only the abstract was read. Self-reported system description, no benchmark.
agent_relevance: Memory reorganisation causes its own retrieval failures: after restructuring the lesson store, old cues can stop finding old lessons. Re-test retrieval after any reorganisation.

source: Lebowitz (1983) Generalization from natural language text, Cognitive Science 7(1)
finding: Abstract: IPP retrieves examples from long-term memory to build generalisations while reading stories, analyses generalisations by components, and checks them against later evidence.
numbers: No numbers in abstract. Full text not opened.
limits: Abstract only. Evaluation was by worked examples, not tests.
agent_relevance: Pattern: generalise from retrieved cases, then test the generalisation on later cases. This matches G3.

source: Wikipedia: Case-based reasoning (history and criticism)
finding: Early CBR came from Schank's Yale group. CYRUS (Kolodner 1983) and IPP (Lebowitz 1983) were the first systems on the dynamic memory model. The only criticism cited: CBR rests on anecdotal evidence, generalisations lack statistical backing.
numbers: No evaluation figures given for early systems.
limits: Encyclopedia summary, secondary source. Page does not name CHEF or MOPs.
agent_relevance: There is no benchmark record for the 1980s systems. Any claim that they worked rests on demos.

source: Wikipedia: Script theory
finding: Schank-Abelson scripts in AI 'ultimately ended without tangible success'. Scripts are inflexible, which motivated memory organisation packets (MOPs). The page gives no human experiments.
numbers: None.
limits: Secondary source. Human script studies are not covered on the page.
agent_relevance: Rigid scripts fail on variants; prefer flexible, case-indexed memory over fixed procedures.

source: Bower, Black & Turner (1979) Scripts in memory for text, Cognitive Psychology 11
finding: From background knowledge, NOT verified this session: people agreed on the main actions of everyday scripts, and in recall and recognition tended to import unstated script actions, supporting script-like structure in human memory.
numbers: Exact percentages not verified. Do not cite numbers from this line.
limits: Evidence is for scripts (generic event schemas), not for episode-indexed MOPs.
agent_relevance: Human data support generic event knowledge, not the specific MOP indexing scheme. Weak support for the design.

source: Reiser, Black & Abelson (1985) Knowledge structures in the organization and retrieval of autobiographical memories, Cognitive Psychology 17
finding: From background knowledge, NOT verified this session: autobiographical retrieval appears to go through general activities (for example going to the dentist) before specific events, taken as support for Schank's idea of events organised under general structures.
numbers: No numbers verified.
limits: Laboratory studies from one group; rival hierarchies exist in later autobiographical-memory work. Not verified here.
agent_relevance: A two-level lesson store (strategy, then instance) is plausible. Test it ourselves.

source: Memento: Fine-tuning LLM Agents without Fine-tuning LLMs (Zhou et al. 2025)
finding: Case-bank memory with a planner and an executor is added to a GPT-4.1 / o4-mini agent without any weight updates. Reached top on GAIA validation and a high test score.
numbers: GAIA validation 87.88% Pass@3 (L1 96.23, L2 90.70, L3 61.54); GAIA test 79.40%; DeepResearcher 66.6 F1 / 80.4 PM; SimpleQA 95.0%; HLE 24.4 PM.
limits: Pass@3 on validation uses a case bank accumulated on that set; the test number is lower. No repeat by others seen.
agent_relevance: Case-based memory without training is a competitive design for tool agents.

source: Memento (Zhou et al. 2025), ablation of case memory
finding: Case memory helps, and most of the total gain on HLE and SimpleQA comes from live tools and the planner-executor split, not from cases.
numbers: HLE avg F1/PM: online executor 11.2/15.8, Memento w/o CBR 22.2/17.4, Memento 26.7/24.4. SimpleQA PM: w/o CBR 89.7, with CBR 95.0. DeepResearcher out-of-distribution gain from cases: +4.7 to +9.6 points.
limits: Case gain is a fraction of the total gain; tool access dominates.
agent_relevance: Do not credit memory for gains that tools or decomposition produced. Always run a no-memory arm with the same scaffold.

source: Memento (Zhou et al. 2025), number of retrieved cases K
finding: More retrieved cases do not help past a small number. Performance peaks at K=4 and plateaus or dips after.
numbers: DeepResearcher avg F1/PM: K=0 59.9/72.2; K=1 63.6/77.9; K=4 64.5/78.5; K=8 64.1/78.2; K=32 63.9/78.1. Over 5 iterations: no-CBR 78.65 to 84.47, parametric CBR 80.46 to 85.44.
limits: Differences among nonzero K are about 1 point. The gap between no-CBR and CBR shrinks from 1.8 to 1.0 points by iteration 5.
agent_relevance: Retrieve a few cases (1 to 4), not many. The edge of memory over no memory shrinks with more rounds.

source: Xiong et al. (2025) How memory management impacts LLM agents: experience-following
finding: Agents copy retrieved experience: high input similarity to a stored record gives high output similarity. Wrong stored records therefore spread errors. Adding everything hurts; adding only checked records helps.
numbers: Success rate or accuracy. RegAgent: fixed 67.53, add-all 55.48, strict 70.95. EHRAgent: fixed 16.75, add-all 13.05, strict 38.50. AgentDriver: fixed 40.11, add-all 32.32, strict 51.00. CIC-IoT: fixed 71.50, add-all 59.90, strict 85.40. RegAgent memory size add-all 4100 vs strict 2938.
limits: Four agents, one synthetic. The strict judge is ground truth or a human label, not available in deployment. Coarse LLM judges were mixed (EHRAgent C1 26.19 vs C3 34.66).
agent_relevance: Store only verified experiences (G2, G3). Unfiltered remember-everything fell 8 to 12 points below a frozen memory.

source: Xiong et al. (2025), memory deletion
finding: Deleting records by downstream utility (history-based) helps with a reliable evaluator. Periodic deletion cuts memory a lot at small cost.
numbers: RegAgent with coarse C1: no deletion 63.18 (3511 records), periodic 60.88 (1012), history 62.10 (3205), combined 59.32 (951). With strict: 70.95 (2938), 67.65 (949), 69.80 (2286), 66.58 (890). Rule: delete if retrieved at least 3 times and mean utility below threshold.
limits: History deletion is unreliable with a noisy judge. On AgentDriver the strict history rule beat an error-free memory baseline.
agent_relevance: Future task outcomes can label stored lessons for free. Prune lessons whose later uses went badly.

source: Ouyang et al. (2025/2026) ReasoningBank
finding: Storing distilled strategy items (title, description, content) from both successes and failures beats raw trajectories (Synapse) and successful workflows (AWM). Success labels come from an LLM judge without ground truth.
numbers: WebArena overall SR, Gemini-2.5-flash: no memory 40.5, Synapse 42.1, AWM 44.1, ReasoningBank 48.8, plus MaTTS 51.8. Steps 9.7 to 8.3. Overall gains +8.3, +7.2, +4.6 for three backbones. Up to 20% relative gain, 16% fewer steps claimed.
limits: Google authors, their own benchmark runs. The Multi subset has 29 tasks (AWM 3.4% there, below no memory 10.3%).
agent_relevance: Abstract lessons transfer better than raw cases, and failures carry signal. AWM fell below no memory on cross-site tasks.

source: Ouyang et al. (2025/2026) ReasoningBank, ablation
finding: Adding failed trajectories raised success. Extra rollouts only help when memory is strong.
numbers: WebArena-Shopping: success-only 46.5 vs with failures 49.7. MaTTS without memory BoN 39.0 to 42.2. Pass@1 with scaling: Synapse 40.6 to 41.2, AWM 44.4 to 45.5, ReasoningBank 49.7 to 53.0. Sequential MaTTS 54.5 vs vanilla 51.9.
limits: Single subset and backbone for the scaling analysis.
agent_relevance: Failure lessons are worth storing; extra samples without good memory are low value (fits G4).

source: Wang et al. (2024) Agent Workflow Memory
finding: Induced reusable workflows raise success on web tasks, online or offline. Wrong workflows can hurt, and train/test task mismatch limits gains.
numbers: +24.6% relative step success on Mind2Web, +51.1% relative success on WebArena (+12.0 points over BrowserGym), and +7.6% over human-written workflows (text elsewhere says 7.9%).
limits: The paper itself says induced workflows are not always correct and can degrade performance when test tasks differ from training. Internal 7.6 vs 7.9 mismatch.
agent_relevance: Workflow memory is brittle across templates; keep a fallback to plain reasoning.

source: Shinn et al. (2023) Reflexion
finding: Verbal reflections stored in an episodic buffer let an agent fix failed tasks on retry. Learning needs a binary success signal from the environment.
numbers: ALFWorld: ReAct+Reflexion solved 130 of 134 tasks over 12 trials. ReAct-only, CoT-only and CoT(GT)-only did not solve any task that failed on trial one when retried at temperature 0.7.
limits: Needs a reliable success signal; the paper notes self-written tests can be flaky and mislead.
agent_relevance: Reflection works with real feedback (G2). Without it the memory piece is unreliable.

source: Zhao et al. (2024) ExpeL
finding: Agent stores trajectories and extracts insights from success/failure pairs. Both retrieval and insights matter; the better mode differs by task.
numbers: Insights-only vs retrieve-only: HotpotQA 36% vs 31%, ALFWorld 50% vs 55%, WebShop 37% vs 38%. ALFWorld ExpeL 59.0 vs ReAct 40.0, random examples 42.5, reasoning-similarity retrieval 48.5. HotpotQA: ReAct 28.0, hand-crafted insights 32.0, insights with reflections 29.0, gpt-3.5 insights 32.0, ExpeL 39.0. Reflexion R3 54% vs ExpeL 59% (ALFWorld).
limits: Four-fold, small sets (100 HotpotQA, 134 ALFWorld, 100 WebShop). Random retrieval nearly erases the gain.
agent_relevance: Retrieve by task similarity, not randomly. Adding raw reflections to insight extraction lowered accuracy.

source: Sourati et al. (2023) Case-based reasoning with language models for classification of logical fallacies
finding: Retrieving similar cases helps classifiers, but not by copying labels. Best variants add counterarguments or explanations to each case.
numbers: CBR beats vanilla by 2.5 to 6 F1 in-domain and up to 8 F1 out-of-domain. Case representation changes F1 by 6 to 8%. Overlap of retrieved labels with true labels only 27.7%. Rare classes: Equivocation 0 to 0.35, Fallacy of Extension 0.48 to 0.75.
limits: Small encoder models, fallacy data only. Surface-similar cases can mislead.
agent_relevance: Retrieved cases act indirectly, so what is stored (the case representation) matters as much as retrieval.

source: Wiratunga et al. (2024) CBR-RAG
finding: Case-structured retrieval for legal QA gives only a small gain. Full-case context beat support-text only in most hybrids.
numbers: Best: hybrid AnglEBERT k=3, about 1.94% higher cosine similarity than No-RAG, significant at 95% vs No-RAG and hybrid LegalBERT. Test set 32 cases. 57% (1,183) of cases cite no legal act.
limits: Tiny test set (32), embedding similarity to a reference as metric, Mistral-7B. No-RAG baseline already high.
agent_relevance: Cheap embedding-based retrieval gains are small. Do not expect retrieval alone to move accuracy much.

source: Wei et al. (2025/2026) Evo-Memory
finding: Benchmark of 10+ memory modules on streaming tasks. Simple ExpRAG often rivals complex designs. Gains track within-dataset task similarity.
numbers: Correlation of ReMem gain with task similarity r=0.717 (Gemini 2.5 Flash) and 0.563 (Claude 3.7 Sonnet). ReMem BabyAI 0.92, ScienceWorld 0.95. ALFWorld steps 22.6 to 11.5.
limits: Gains are smaller on diverse sets (AIME-25, GPQA). ReMem is the authors' own method; no independent check.
agent_relevance: Memory pays off when tasks recur in structure; on one-off diverse problems expect little.

source: Wei et al. (2025/2026) Evo-Memory, failure experiences and order
finding: Storing both successes and failures without filtering degrades baselines. Memory with refinement stays robust. Task order (easy to hard vs hard to easy) changes results.
numbers: Baselines 'suffer notable degradation under unfiltered failures'. ExpRAG easy-to-hard 0.77/0.87/0.37 vs hard-to-easy 0.87/0.92/0.51 (values as printed in text extraction).
limits: Table columns hard to read from text extraction; direction is clear, exact values should be rechecked in the paper.
agent_relevance: Order of tasks changes memory value; label failures before storing them.

source: Suzgun et al. (2025) Dynamic Cheatsheet
finding: Test-time memory of strategies and code. Big gains for strong models on recurring-structure tasks; none or negative for small models.
numbers: Claude 3.5 Sonnet AIME 2024 23% to 50%; AIME 2025 +30 points; GPQA-Diamond +9. GPT-4o Game of 24 10% to 99%. Claude 3.5 Haiku AIME24 10.0 to 36.7. GPT-4o-mini AIME24 16.7 to 13.3 (DC-Cu). Haiku GPQA baseline 43.4, DC- 41.9, DC-RS 49.0. Majority vote of 3 on Sonnet: no gain (23.3%).
limits: AIME sets are 30 questions each, so one question is 3.3 points. Small models misapply retrieved knowledge; DC-RS dipped GPT-4o on GPQA from bad retrieval.
agent_relevance: Memory gains depend on model strength and task similarity; small models can be hurt.

source: Park et al. (2023) Generative agents
finding: Memory stream with observation, planning and reflection. Removing parts lowers human-rated believability in order.
numbers: TrueSkill: full 29.89 (sd 0.72); no reflection 26.88; no reflection or planning 25.64; crowdworker 22.95; no memory 21.21. Kruskal-Wallis chi2(4)=150.29, p<0.001; 100 rank sets.
limits: Believability ratings, not task success. Agents also embellished memories and retrieved incomplete fragments.
agent_relevance: Reflection helps synthesis across episodes; partial retrieval can produce confident wrong answers.

source: Wu et al. (2025) LongMemEval
finding: Memory systems for chat assistants lose a lot against reading the full history. Design choices (session decomposition, fact-augmented keys, time-aware queries) recover part of it.
numbers: 500 questions. About 30% accuracy drop for commercial assistants and long-context models; ChatGPT (GPT-4o) 37% and Coze 64% drop vs offline reading. Even with oracle retrieval, a poor reading strategy loses up to 10 points.
limits: Conversational recall, not experience reuse. Commercial systems tested on a 97-question sample.
agent_relevance: Index granularity and reading format change accuracy; use an oracle-retrieval arm to separate retrieval from reading.

source: Chhikara et al. (2025) Mem0
finding: Extracted-memory systems approach but do not beat full-context reading on LOCOMO accuracy, with large latency savings.
numbers: LLM-judge overall: full-context 72.90%, Mem0g 68.44%, RAG range 36.8 to 60.97. Mem0 91% lower latency than full-context. Zep best on open-domain (J 76.60 vs Mem0g 75.71).
limits: Vendor paper; A-Mem was re-run by the authors, so baselines may be under-tuned. 10 conversations.
agent_relevance: Compression costs a few points of accuracy. If context fits, full text beats memory.

source: Xu et al. (2025) A-Mem
finding: Linked, self-organising notes claimed to beat MemGPT, MemoryBank and ReadAgent on LoCoMo. A rival paper re-ran it and found it far behind.
numbers: Mem0 authors report A-Mem lags by more than 25 J points when re-run under a judge. A-Mem exact F1 values not extracted here.
limits: Self-reported win vs rival re-run loss. Unresolved.
agent_relevance: Self-organising memory results are not reproducible across labs yet.

source: Sumers et al. (2024) CoALA
finding: Frames language agents with working, episodic, semantic and procedural memory. Notes that writing to procedural memory is riskier than writing to episodic or semantic memory.
numbers: No new experiments.
limits: Survey and framework.
agent_relevance: Do not let the agent rewrite its core procedure from one episode; write to episodic first.
